questions.text: A Marshallian demand function gives the optimal quantity of a good as a function of

options.a: the quantities of other consumers only.
options.b: production costs only.
options.d: utility level only.

questions.text: Comparative statics of demand studies

options.a: how firms choose production technology.
options.b: how utility numbers change under monotonic transformations.
options.c: only the time path of adjustment between two market equilibria.
options.d: how optimal choices change when prices or income change.

questions.text: A normal good is one for which, holding prices fixed, demand

options.a: is independent of income by definition.
options.b: increases when income increases.
options.d: increases when its own price increases.

questions.text: An inferior good is one for which, over the relevant income range, demand

options.a: is always zero.
options.b: must increase when its own price rises.
options.d: decreases when income increases.

questions.text: Whether a good is inferior can depend on

options.a: whether the good is discrete.
options.b: the consumer’s income level and the relevant range being considered.
options.c: whether the consumer has complete preferences.
options.d: only the sign of its market price.

questions.text: The income offer curve traces

options.a: market equilibria as supply shifts.
options.b: the utility-maximizing bundles chosen at different income levels, holding prices fixed.
options.c: bundles with equal expenditure but different preferences.
options.d: the quantities chosen at different own prices, holding income fixed.

questions.text: Another name for the income offer curve is the

options.a: income expansion path.
options.b: compensated supply path.
options.d: price offer curve.

questions.text: An Engel curve plots

options.a: the utility level against both quantities.
options.b: the demand for one good against income, holding prices fixed.
options.c: the price of one good against the price of another good.
options.d: the price of one good against the quantity demanded, holding income fixed.

questions.text: If both goods are normal, the income expansion path generally has

options.a: a positive slope in (x1,x2) space.
options.b: a vertical slope necessarily.
options.d: a negative slope necessarily.

questions.text: For Cobb-Douglas utility u=x1^a x2^(1−a), demand for good 1 is

options.b: x1 = a m/p1.

questions.text: For Cobb-Douglas preferences, Marshallian demands are linear in income, so

options.a: Engel curves are necessarily vertical.
options.b: the price offer curve is always horizontal.
options.d: Engel curves are straight lines through the origin.

questions.text: A luxury good is one for which demand

options.a: falls when income rises.
options.b: rises by a greater proportion than income.
options.d: rises by a smaller proportion than income.

questions.text: A necessary good, in the terminology of the slides, is one for which demand

options.a: rises by a smaller proportion than income.
options.b: rises by a greater proportion than income.
options.d: must have unit income elasticity exactly.

questions.text: Preferences are homothetic if scaling both bundles by the same positive factor

options.a: changes the relative price of the goods.
options.b: makes the consumer indifferent between them.
options.d: reverses their preference ranking.

questions.text: With homothetic preferences, if income is multiplied by t while prices are fixed, the demanded bundle

options.a: is divided by t.
options.b: must move to a boundary solution.
options.d: is multiplied by t.

questions.text: A key implication of homothetic preferences is that

options.a: the MRS is constant at all bundles.
options.b: every good is inferior.
options.c: income offer curves and Engel curves are straight lines through the origin.
options.d: own-price demand slopes upward.

Under quasilinear preferences, interior demand for good 1 is independent of income because

options.a: income enters utility after substitution only as an additive constant with respect to x1.
options.b: good 1 is always inferior.
options.c: the price ratio changes one-for-one with income.
options.d: the budget constraint does not contain income.

questions.text: For quasilinear preferences, the Engel curve for good 1 is vertical over the interior range because

options.a: changing income does not change the chosen x1.
options.b: good 1 has zero price.
options.d: x1 must always equal x2.

An ordinary good, as defined in the price-demand discussion, has demand that

options.a: is independent of its own price.
options.b: decreases when its own price decreases.
options.c: increases when its own price decreases.
options.d: must also be an inferior good.

questions.text: A Giffen good is unusual because

options.a: its demand is independent of price.
options.b: it must be a luxury good.
options.d: its demand decreases when its own price decreases, over the relevant range.

questions.text: For an ordinary good, the own-price derivative typically satisfies

options.a: dx1/dp1 = m.
options.b: dx1/dp1 < 0.
options.d: dx1/dp1 = 1.

questions.text: The price offer curve for good 1 traces

options.a: bundles along a single indifference curve as utility is held fixed.
options.b: utility-maximizing bundles as p1 varies while p2 and income are held fixed.
options.c: utility-maximizing bundles as income varies while both prices are fixed.
options.d: market supply as all input prices vary.

questions.text: The ordinary demand curve for good 1 plots

options.a: x2 as a function of income only.
options.b: utility as a function of x1.
options.c: x1 as a function of p1, holding p2 and income fixed.
options.d: p2 as a function of x2.

questions.text: For one-for-one perfect substitutes, if p1 > p2, demand for good 1 is

options.a: m/p2.
options.d: m/p1.

questions.text: For one-for-one perfect substitutes, if p1 < p2, demand for good 1 is

options.b: zero.
options.d: m/p1.

questions.text: For perfect complements u=min(x1,x2), demand for good 1 is

options.a: m/p2.
options.d: m/p1.

questions.text: For a discrete good, a reservation price for the nth unit is

options.a: the minimum legal price for the good.
options.b: the price at which the consumer is just indifferent between buying the nth unit and not buying it.
options.c: the market-clearing price of the entire industry.
options.d: the price of the composite good.

questions.text: A discrete-good demand curve can be represented by

options.a: only an Engel curve, never a price-quantity relation.
options.b: a single smooth horizontal line.
options.c: a vertical line independent of preferences.
options.d: a sequence of reservation-price thresholds at which quantity demanded jumps by units.

questions.text: Good 1 is a substitute for good 2 if, holding other determinants fixed,

options.a: demand for good 1 falls when the price of good 2 rises.
options.b: demand for good 1 is independent of all prices.
options.c: demand for good 1 rises when the price of good 2 rises.
options.d: demand for good 1 rises when its own price rises.

questions.text: Good 1 is a complement to good 2 if

options.a: demand for good 1 falls when the price of good 2 rises.
options.b: both goods have identical prices.
options.d: demand for good 1 rises when the price of good 2 rises.

questions.text: The inverse demand function expresses

options.a: quantity demanded as a function of price only.
options.b: income as a function of utility.
options.c: price as a function of quantity demanded.
options.d: utility as a function of prices and income.

questions.text: If Cobb-Douglas demand for good 1 is x1 = am/p1, the inverse demand is

options.a: p1 = am/x1.
options.b: p1 = am x1.

questions.text: At an interior optimum, inverse demand is related to marginal willingness to pay by

options.a: p1 = p2|MRS|.
options.b: p1 + p2 = |MRS|.
options.d: p1 = p2/|MRS| always.

questions.text: If good 2 is money with p2=1, the inverse demand curve for good 1 measures

options.a: the consumer’s marginal willingness to pay for additional units of good 1.
options.b: the marginal utility of money multiplied by income.
options.c: the average production cost of good 1.
options.d: the consumer’s total income at each quantity.

questions.text: A downward-sloping inverse demand curve means that

options.a: marginal willingness to pay rises with consumption.
options.b: the good must be Giffen.
options.c: the consumer’s income is falling along the curve.
options.d: marginal willingness to pay declines as consumption of the good increases.

questions.text: Refer to the accompanying figure. Which behavior identifies good 1 as Giffen in the figure?

options.a: When the price of good 1 decreases, the chosen quantity of good 1 also decreases.
options.b: Demand for good 1 increases only because income rises.
options.c: When the price of good 1 decreases, the chosen quantity of good 1 increases.
options.d: Demand for good 1 is unchanged when its price changes.
